analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring schools to inspect for and manage asbestos.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee, and the 1986 asbestos-inspection rules for schools stayed in force.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act of 1986, the law that requires public and private schools to inspect their buildings for asbestos and carry out plans to keep students and staff from breathing it. It would also order the EPA to spend 18 months studying the two forms of asbestos and report back to Congress. In the meantime, schools would have no federal asbestos rules at all.
analysis.who_benefits: School districts that would no longer have to pay for asbestos inspections and management plans, and asbestos product makers who would face less federal scrutiny of the fibers in their materials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: School districts and asbestos product makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act of 1986 and the asbestos provisions of the Toxic Substances Control Act, lifting the federal requirement that schools inspect for asbestos and manage it [S2][S3].
Directs the EPA to study the health hazards of serpentine and amphibole asbestos fibers and report findings and recommendations to Congress within 18 months [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Schoolchildren, teachers, and school staff, who would work and learn in buildings where asbestos hazards no longer have to be found or managed.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the only federal requirement that schools identify asbestos-containing material and manage it, leaving students and staff unprotected during and after the 18-month EPA study [S2][S3].

The good-faith objection from supporters: the 1986 law imposes real inspection and management costs on local school districts, and supporters argued those costs should wait for the results of a fresh scientific study of the two fiber types [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings go to school district budgets; the risk lands on the people inside the buildings. Even a supporter would have to admit the bill removes protections first and studies the science second, an 18-month gap with no federal school asbestos rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1991, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Craig Thomas of Wyoming introduced the bill on March 7, 1990, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
Ten House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
On March 14, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with no further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schoolchildren, teachers, and staff are better off because the bill died: the 1986 law still required schools to find and manage asbestos in their buildings, and the inspection and abatement firms that do that work kept their mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schoolchildren and staff kept asbestos protections

for.name: Rep. Craig Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 1986 asbestos rules for schools on March 7, 1990

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 101st Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and never reported it out or scheduled a hearing or vote

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Repealing the 1986 act would end the federal program that identifies asbestos hazards in school buildings and would replace scrutiny of both fiber types with a multi-year study. Less federal attention to asbestos in buildings means less exposure risk traced back to their products.

These firms perform the inspections, monitoring, and removal work the 1986 law requires schools to do. Repeal would erase that line of business, and their interest ran with keeping school buildings safe.

Repeal would lift the federal mandate to inspect and manage asbestos, freeing school budgets from those costs. The saving is real, but it would come at the expense of the students and staff inside the buildings.
